results.observation_summary:
Traveled from Commonwealth TH along the usual approach, up to the bottom of the avy swath, over to middle Kendall Peak Lake, and then back out to Commonwealth TH via Kendall Knob.  Snow in the trees was soft and deep.  The soft snow made for enjoyable skiing but arduous skinning where we had to set a track.  Full solar aspects in the open had a substantial crust that was less noticeable on more shaded aspects.

We kept our travel largely in the trees with a conservative mindset, and the observed crust kept us from stepping out into more open areas.  No signs of instability observed.

results.name: Observer Name
results.route: We traveled from Silverstar snowpark via snowmobiles past Washington Pass. We started climbing on skis at 5000ft, ascending primarily westerly aspects to 6700ft.
results.instability_summary:
There was evidence of a widespread natural dry loose and wind slab avalanche cycle estimated to be about 48 hours old, during peak wind and snow on 3/13/26. We could push stubborn, dry, loose slides on very steep test slopes, and we observed one very, very small wind slab below a cliff band, triggered by loose snow from above. 

Wind-loaded test slopes would produce isolated cracking.
results.observation_summary:
Other than a frigid start to the morning, it was an overall pleasant day with light winds and overcast skies. We found minor instabilities within the new snow in wind-loaded areas, which were enough to keep us in sheltered lower-angle terrain. We watched one tiny wind slab release from very steep terrain below cliffs. It was triggered by loose snow sliding down the cliff face. Steep test slopes in sheltered locations produced small dry loose avalanches, but they didn't tend to run far or fast. Stability tests showed some weaknesses in the upper snowpack, but we didn't observe any signs of instability outside of wind-loaded slopes.

The extent of the natural avalanche cycle from Friday (3/13/2026) was impressive. While none of the avalanches were very large, pretty much any steep slope showed evidence of either dry loose or slab avalanches.

advanced_fields.weather_summary: The morning started out bitterly cold with moderate westerly winds. Winds died down by mid-morning and temperatures moderated to just chilly by midday. Skies were overcast, with thin clouds in the morning becoming thicker as the day progressed. Light snow began around 2:00 pm.
advanced_fields.snowpack_summary:
Snow Surface Summary
Deep, dry snow everywhere in sheltered terrain. There was 5cm of snow in the last 24 hours. Boot penetration was 40-50cm, and ski penetration was 20-30cm. In more wind-exposed terrain, recent snow had been drifted around, and snow depths varied between 4-5" up to 2'. Any slopes exposed to large avalanche paths above had soft avalanche debris with 5-6" of snow on top. Recent snow depths were fairly consistent from 5000ft-6700ft, only variable due to wind exposure. 

Snowpack Summary
50-60cm of recent snow overlays the 3/8 melt-freeze crust. Within the recent snow, a density change exists from warming and strong winds down about 30cm. Stability tests yielded stubborn results beneath this harder layer on a layer of softer, preserved precipitation particles and decomposing fragments. The overlying snow showed a favorable bond to the 3/8 crust, which is pencil to knife hard. Below the crust is a weak layer of .5-1mm faceted melt-forms. Below this, the snowpack consists of multiple layers of melt-freeze crusts, with some weaker, rounded facets between melt layers. 

On wind loaded slopes, hand shears failed easily with moderate effort in the upper 20cm of wind drifted snow.

results.name: Observer Name
results.observation_summary:
Plan A was powder laps at Hyak, a plan a parking-lot full of others had, too.  As soon as our skis touched snow, it became clear that yesterday's heavy pow was now beneath a fully boot-supportable crust at pass-level.  New plans were made and rapidly discarded due to intense parking-lot crowding. Plan E became a long skin in the woods with friends to 5,000', which turned out to be better than Plan A.

The crust was completely gone before we reached 4,000'. Calm winds, filtered (decreasing) sunshine, and long views were all very fine.  Trail-breaking on fattest skis remained boot-top. Tree wells in thick trees still grabbed at our skis.
     Settlement-cones were evident everywhere, especially at upper elevations.  Walking the crests of test slopes got no obvious response.
     A few tree bombs falling, but trees mostly still hold their snow all the way to the ridgetops.

For the initial descent, we selected a familiar SE slope of sheltered forest. Ski quality was great. No instability noted.
    Returning to Pass level, the crust had softened, but to our surprise, was still supportable around 3pm.

Very grateful for this brief return to true winter as we all know it. Even a fleeting chance to let pow skis run on bottomless hometown snow can fill the soul.

results.observation_summary:
Pleasant day of skiing and observing. Found about a foot of new snow on top of a crust that made for pleasant riding conditions. Found that non polar aspects could have a slight crust but it was mostly avoidable and thin.

Pit - dug a pit 85cm down on a NNW aspect just down from artist point at 4740 feet. Snow profile shown below. 30-40cm down was around 4 degrees colder than air temp. Found mostly  dry decomposing fragments below the 3/12 melt freeze and wet decomposing fragments below it. Both CT and ECT failed 5cm down on only a few taps. The failures were non planar and irregular, with no energy. No other failures were observed.

results.name: Observer Name
results.observation_summary:
Not many signs of instability anywhere. Most places prone to avalanches already had one come down previously. There was a slight sun crust despite the bowl being 5600-6400' and north facing. Ski pen was as high was 50cm in many places. I tried to skin up old avy chutes as ski pen was only 10-20cm in them.
The bowl was good skiing and stability was very good. I did a profile at 6400', which was were I skied down from. Grains were mostly rounded in the lower pack as the temperature gradient has been very low. The moist melt formations found in the lower pack were not present at this elevation. The snow height there was 410cm (161in), which seemed like quite a good pack for how poor the season has been.

advanced_fields.weather_summary: Cool, calm, mostly thin overcast with occasional patches of blue sky. No new snow.
advanced_fields.snowpack_summary:
The height of snow doubled with over 1 meter of settled storm snow from March 8-13th. The hardness profile is generally right-side-up, progressing from softer to harder. Boot Penetration is 50-80cm with ski penetration ~40cm. Trailbreaking is still relatively deep. We saw significant signs of settlement, including large settlement cones with cracks and wrinkles near depressions and features.

Where observed, layers in the upper snowpack are well-bonded, including to both the 3/12 crust, ↓60-80cm, and the 3/8 crust, ↓110-120cm. A slight weak layer exists above the 3/8 crust, but it's generally not problematic, and didn't produce test results. The old mid-Feb cruts/weak layers, ↓130-160cm, have transformed into melt forms and are mostly unrecognizable. Of note, for the upcoming rain/wetting, there's a relatively thick, weak layer of moist, 4Finger-4F+ hard melt forms about 150cm below the surface.

See profile graph from E, 5380ft.
